claim: Hammoud, Khadiv, and Righetti extend iterative risk-sensitive optimal control to multi-contact legged locomotion with measurement uncertainty and use its local state-feedback matrices as automatically optimized stiffness and damping schedules. A Gaussian uncertainty ellipsoid at an impending foot contact is mapped into full robot state space and projected into the null space of active contacts; with positive risk sensitivity, the optimizer trades tracking accuracy for lower gains and impact robustness. Solo quadruped simulations report lower unexpected-contact force, approximately 20% lower jump impact force, admissible gain magnitudes, and more successful trotting across randomized terrain than standard DDP. These are simulation-only, locally optimal results under a predefined contact schedule, chosen covariance model, rigid-contact planning model, and tuned simulator; no theorem establishes closed-loop contact stability, constraint satisfaction under true uncertainty, global optimality, or transfer to hardware, and two alternative uncertainty models perform worse than DDP after impact.
claim_locator: Section IV-C, Table I and Figures 10-11
epistemic_status: qualified primary simulation evidence: the stochastic optimal-control and contact-noise formulation is explicit, but performance claims come solely from one modeled quadruped and local iterative solutions; stability, real-world calibration, and hardware feasibility are not demonstrated
problem_and_setting: High-gain locomotion feedback rejects disturbances but can generate destabilizing force at unexpected contact, while excessive compliance sacrifices task tracking. The paper seeks a systematic way to optimize time-varying whole-body feedback gains that reason jointly about process noise, state-estimation uncertainty, and uncertain foot-contact location during stepping, jumping, and trotting.
method_or_mechanism: The method uses rigid multi-contact dynamics with predefined contact phases and an exponential risk-sensitive cost. Local dynamics and cost approximations support an iterative Riccati-like backward pass. Measurement uncertainty is incorporated by augmenting the linearized robot deviations with error-state EKF dynamics; the resulting control law depends on the conditional state estimate. Contact-location uncertainty is represented as Gaussian position/velocity noise at the swing foot, mapped through a pseudoinverse into robot state space, and projected into the null space of feet already in rigid contact before being added to ordinary state-measurement covariance. A positive risk parameter penalizes higher cost moments and changes the full local feedback matrices, whose position and velocity blocks are interpreted as stiffness and damping schedules.
content_summary: A kino-dynamic optimizer first supplies reference trajectories and contact timing. Standard DDP and risk-sensitive optimization then share the same costs, nominal states, feedforward torques, and flat-floor plan; only the feedback gains differ, with risk sensitivity sigma=10 and fixed Gaussian covariances. Simulations use a detailed Solo quadruped model at 1 kHz, a 0.01 s optimization grid, and a stiff linear spring-damper contact simulator. In an 8 cm step, an unplanned 3 cm block causes early contact. Uniform and swing-joint noise models diverge, whereas contact-space uncertainty, especially after null-space projection, produces much smaller gain norms and impact forces. In a 0.5 m jump with an unexpected 3 cm block, the risk-sensitive policy increases joint damping and reports 20% lower impact force but larger position error. A 14-switch trot is tested in 1000 simulations divided between terrain disturbances up to 14% and 11% of leg length; the paper reports more successful terminal executions than DDP while accepting larger base tracking error.
synthesis_role: Represents uncertainty-aware offline impedance optimization for dynamic contact rather than online force-error adaptation. It shows how covariance structure can induce compliant and dissipative gain patterns, but also exposes the dependence of risk-sensitive behavior on the correctness of the selected noise model.
development_link: The work brings Ponton's measurement-uncertainty risk-sensitive formulation into whole-body multi-contact control and complements deterministic variable-impedance methods by optimizing full feedback matrices. Unlike passivity filters or energy bounds, its robustness is objective- and distribution-driven rather than certified by an interaction-energy inequality.

evidence.finding: An exponential cost incorporates higher cost moments, and augmented EKF/error dynamics make local feedback gains depend on process and measurement covariance.
The nonlinear problem is split across predefined smooth contact phases, while an error-state EKF on the floating-base manifold is included in each local iteration.
Swing-foot contact-location covariance is mapped to full state space and projected into the active-contact null space so it does not contradict rigid support constraints.

DDP and risk-sensitive controllers use identical costs, reference trajectories, nominal feedforward torques, and flat-ground planning; risk sensitivity and the assumed covariance model determine the gain differences.

For an early foot strike, uniform and swing-joint risk models diverge after impact, while contact-space models lower gains and forces; the null-space-projected model best preserves support-foot behavior.
Risk-sensitive control raises joint damping before unexpected landing, reports 20% lower impact force and avoids DDP bouncing, at the cost of larger joint-position deviations.

evidence.locator: Section IV-C, Table I and Figures 10-11
evidence.finding: Across 1000 randomized trotting simulations in two terrain-amplitude batches, the risk-sensitive policy is reported to finish successfully more often than DDP but with larger tracking errors when successful.
All validation is numerical; the authors identify real-robot experiments as future work.

boundary_conditions: The optimized solution is local, initialized from a separate kino-dynamic plan, and uses a predefined contact sequence and timing.

Rigid contact is assumed inside the optimizer, while validation uses a particular linear spring-damper contact simulator; complementarity, slip transitions, and contact-model mismatch are not formally addressed.
Noise is Gaussian with manually chosen covariances and fixed risk sensitivity; the behavior changes materially with the structure and magnitude of that covariance.
Feedback blocks are interpreted as impedance schedules but are full local gain matrices and need not correspond to a passive, symmetric, independently realizable Cartesian mass-spring-damper.
No passivity, Lyapunov stability, chance-constraint, recursive feasibility, collision-safety, torque-limit, or global-optimality guarantee is derived for the executed policy.
All evidence uses one simulated Solo quadruped and one simulator parameterization; statements that gains are hardware-admissible rely on preliminary experience, not robot experiments.
DDP and risk-sensitive methods share references and costs, but comparison covers one baseline family and one selected risk parameter rather than a broad robustness benchmark.
The 1000-run success comparison is reported without confidence intervals, sensitivity analysis over simulator uncertainty, or independent replication.
assumptions: Local linear-quadratic approximations and the iterative solver converge to a useful policy around the supplied nominal trajectory.
The error-state EKF is observable and its Gaussian covariance adequately represents estimation error.
The projected swing-foot covariance is a meaningful proxy for unknown terrain height and contact timing.
The nominal contact sequence remains valid under disturbances large enough to test robustness.
The simulator's stiffness, damping, friction, integration step, and robot model approximate the relevant impact dynamics.
Positive exponential risk sensitivity creates the desired accuracy-robustness tradeoff without excessive conservatism or numerical failure.

reported: Risk-Uniform and Risk-SwingJoints policies diverge after unexpected impact and accumulate more error than DDP.
DDP also diverges in the early-contact example and produces gain magnitudes considered unusable on the real robot.
Risk-sensitive jumping reduces impact but increases joint-position deviation.
Successful risk-sensitive trotting ends with larger base-configuration error in exchange for more successful executions.
Hardware validation is absent and explicitly deferred to future work.
inferred: A miscalibrated covariance or risk parameter can produce inappropriate compliance, excessive tracking error, or worse impact behavior than risk-neutral DDP.
A contact disturbance that changes the mode sequence rather than only its timing/location can invalidate the predefined hybrid plan.
Local gain matrices may exceed actuator bandwidth or violate passivity even when their magnitudes lie in an empirically acceptable range.
The reported Monte Carlo improvement may depend strongly on the same simulator and disturbance distribution used to motivate the uncertainty model.
